The Humboldt Standard, July 28, 1914, stated: "Instead of these being flat points here and there his [Freeman's] work will form a complete panorama of the route in the form of a 'motion picture' of the trip. 000408_202005: Silent black-and-white home movies: 1930s cars on residential streets, family gatherings, boating and swimming on lakes and rivers, rural scenes and Niagara Falls.

rv: A family piles into their 1933 Ford Sedan (with no other cars on their street) for a little trip. Cut to a fine-looking steam locomotive approaching the station. Is everything abandoned? There are shots of an empty farm and a vacant schoolhouse. There's a nice exterior shot of a general store that sells Salada Tea. Several scenes feature a lake, one with a ferry on it. Look! Daddy and uncle somebody caught some frogs. The lakeside cottage has a tree in the middle of the steps. Dad's smoking a cigarette wading in the lake. Back we go to town. There's a nice convertible with the top up and a…

0932_Jack_and_the_Beanstalk_00_46_40_13: Jack exchanges his cow for some magic beans. The beans grow overnight into a beanstalk, which Jack climbs, arriving at a castle that is his. Jack sets a deal with the giant in exchange for their fortune.

rv: The last reel of this silent production of this classic fairy tale has plenty of surprises up its sleeves. Now I'm not an expert on the fairy tale, but I don't remember jack leading an army to fight the giant to save the princess. But nevertheless this altered story line seems to work. This early Fox feature has money put into it, as evidenced by the giants castle, Still, I'm not in any hurry to see the first two reels.

chasing_trouble_ipod: A delivery boy for a flower shop, who thinks of himself as an amateur detective, finds out that his boss is mixed up with a foreign espionage ring.

rv: This film isn't bad. I too watched this because of Mantan Moreland (the black actor). (Somebody here said "the ending is missing," but don't worry about this: a few frames are missing, but what's there is obvious.)
The movie was fun to watch, but part of the ending is missing.

Almost six minutes are missing from this damaged print. Lost are most of the ending and some of Mantan's best stuff. Years ago I saw the complete film on 16mm, and thought it was one of Moreland's and Darro's best. Unfortunately the same can't be said for this truncated version.

chasing_trouble_ipod.tg: FRANKIE'S IN TROUBLE AGAIN… and this time it's MURDER!

WorldThr1957: Moments in aviation history, told through postage stamps.

rv: Totally fun overview of the history of airplanes, told, yes, through stamps! My God! What a great idea! I LOVED this film! The film uses both archival clips and the stamps to weave our way through history. The narrator seems to love this idea too. Its quite obvious that this was a series, and I would like to see more of this pleaaaaaaaaase!! (Hint Hint Rick!) This is a MUST see on this site!

This film appears to be a syndicated 15 minute TV show from 1953 about the stories on stamps. This episode is called "New Horizons For Old" and covers primarily Lindbergh's flight across the Atlantic in 1927. The piece starts off talking about early attempts at long distance flights before World War I. It also talks about how the US government was only one that would bankroll airplanes and developed the first airmail routes in 1918. They also show an example of the first airmail stamp, along with the infamous "upside down Jenny" stamp, which they quote as being worth $4000 (and now worth…

Henry’s brother-in-law takes to stealing his chair and cigarettes but the last straw comes when, in a display of boxing prowess, he knocks his host out cold.
1925LeCuirassPotemkineBronenosetsPotyomk: Sergei Eisenstein's dramatization of the 1905 mutiny aboard the Russian battleship Potemkin, in which sailors rise against their officers and the people of Odessa rally to them, leading to the massacre on the Odessa Steps.
OurGangUncleTomsUncle1926: The Our Gang kids stage their own version of Uncle Tom's Cabin.
fourStarRevue-16May1951: An episode of the comedy-variety series Four Star Revue, starring Jimmy Durante and Fred Allen with a surprise guest. The original commercials are included, one of them featuring Abe Vigoda.

ManhattanWat: Travelogue documentary about Manhattan, New York City distributed by RKO Radio Pictures and produced by the Van Beuren Corporation. Part of the World on Parade series.

rv: Go to  Manhattan: See the homeless!

Curious doc about the landmarks littering Manhattan's shorelines. We see the usual, tugboats, large ships, the stockyards, the fish market and the Brooklyn Bridge. But then the film sort of turns dark and explores the seedier side, with many images of the homeless and some derilct shelters built. Kind of makes you wonder what the whole purpose of this is. Definitely not a travelogue, a little too fluffy to be a social statement..

Unexpectedly, this film shows the grim side of industry with shacks that people live in and also scoffs at wealthy waterfront homes as pretentious. Great shots of a variety of vessels and the fish market.

In the same series as Bounty Paper Towels, this commercial features a housewife and a little girl who are both vexed by a dog that tracks in mud. Since they're not nearly as brain-dead as the couple in the other commercial, this isn't nearly as much fun. But it does still have the jaw-dropping schlurrrrppppp special effect. Ratings: Camp/Humor Value: ****. Weirdness: ***. Historical Interest: ****. Overall Rating: ****.

TellItLikeItIs1964: A television documentary on the Volunteer Improvement Program for illiterate adults in St. Louis, where volunteers at the Hamilton School and St. Regis Catholic Church teach reading, writing and arithmetic. Students, directors and volunteers describe the program and the jobs it opens, and businesses are urged to give space, contributions and scholarships.
1927-a-ship-of-oranges-noburo-ofuji: An animated film about the Edo-period merchant Kinokuniya Bunzaemon, who shipped oranges from Kishu to Edo and made a fortune. Directed by Noburō Ōfuji.
OurHomeT1954: Advertising film presenting landmarks, businesses and people of a Philadelphia suburb.

rv: Damn. Someone already called it, 'a hoot', which was what I was going to say. Anyway, blaring Marines theme and then of course the holy-roller scene aside, this film is wonderful! A bit of background from the narrator, scenery ever-so-lovely and shot rather well (cameraman has an excellent sense of composition!), loved it. I also really appreciate the personal story from, my apologies if I get this wrong, SmallTownBoy; what a delightful portal through spacetime. Thank you, whomever you are!

What a trip! Of *course* it's boring -- it's a fifteen minute advertisement! And in B&W. And a half-century old to boot! But if "you were there," or your parents or grandparents were, then it's a hoot! Like a time machine. Better than a photo album. But what? No Ed's Diner? No Hobby Shop?? At least they caught us coming out of Central Buck Joint High School (NOT West!). Two thumbz up! ;)

Nothing is really interesting in this film. The towns are not picturesque, there are no special places to make the towns distinctive, and except for the movie theatre shown- no recreational facilities or places to go to. This black and white 1954 movie is totally mediocre. It is very poorly directed,filmed and edited.. The 2nd narrator spoke terribly and shouldn't have been used. All the waving of the people made them look awkward. "Our Home Town" was obviously made for the 1954 movie audience of the towns shown.

it's so weird to see Doylestown 50 years ago. My mom is from the lower Bucks area and we have spent a lot of time in Doylestown. It's interesting to see what she saw as a kid. Noticeably absent, though, is Fonthill. In fact, I'm wondering if they just used a random all-purpose soundtrack and just showed random shots of Doylestown to fill in. It is oddly generic. How can you talk about Doylestown without showing Fonthill or the Mercer Museum? Very odd, and too dull for my curiosity about this neat town.

rhkratzse--Yeah, I remember Ed's Diner. Some of the time anyway! Drinking coffee at 4:00AM on a Friday night. Pancho, the chief cook and bottle washer. "Everybody's chewing!" I was a little too young to go to Central Bucks Joint High, though. I went to Unami JR High. I remember the hobby shop, alright. On West State, just east of the 6 point intersection of Clinton, Court, and State? And of course, who could forget Kenny's? Haha, those were good old times. [The following was posted Nov 13, 2007:] One evening in the early 90's I was leaving the lobby of the County Theater, Doylestown, Pa; my…

Miracleo1956_2: Panoramic exploration of cans and canning in the United States, with excellent imagery of mass production and agribusiness.

rv: The film is in the can!

If you've ever wondered why there hasnt been an overflow of Can documentaries, well, look no further. 'Miracle Of The Can' pretty much is the beginning, middle and end of the can. For 40 minutes (!!) we see the birth and the progress of the can in terms of production. If this all sounds pretty boring to you, well, you're sort of right. This film could EASILY be trimmed in half.As a matter of fact, when you've finished the first half, you feel that they've summed it up nicely, then you realize you've got 20 minutes more to go! Only worth seeing for the bizarre shot of cans growing on trees…

0670_Coffee_Break_02_38_41_00: A film about the issue of coffee breaks in the workplace. The film is focused on the cost of coffee breaks and the possibility of reducing the length of the breaks to save money. The participants discuss various perspectives, including the importance of breaks for workers, the need for rules and regulations, and the potential benefits of coffee breaks for team building and socializing. The film also touches on other issues, such as workers taking longer breaks to smoke or apply makeup.

rv: My Dad was an Art Director for Calvin at this time. He was in charge of putting together the sets and props. The drawing that gets coffee spilled all over it definitely one of his drawings, and the tall paintings of Shakespearean caricatures hanging in the ladie's lounge hung in our front entryway of our house for years and currently are hanging in my sister's house! My Dad worked with the director Robert Altman and film editor Lou Lombardo at Calvin. They were good friends.

rv: The highlight of this movie is the trip to an S&H Green Stamp outlet in a mid-fifties classic car. The classic purchase at those stores btw were card tables (chairs extra). I forget how many books it took, Starts out with a premature engagement party, a fight, a make up scene, and ultimately, an engagement. All thanks to S&H Green Stamps! Classic 1957! Everybody in the neighborhood was white! Those WERE the days!

all-that-money-can-buy-1941.tg: A GREAT MOTION PICTURE DARES TO BE DIFFERENT!

TodayShow11201957: The “The Today show” show from Nov. 20 1957, with host Dave Garroway.

rv: One forgets how grim the news was in the supposedly idyllic 1950s. Nothing but war and the threat of war. Everyone arming themselves with nuclear missiles. And how cruddy everyone looked! Everyone looked 50+ and wore dumpy clothes. Perhaps it's the grayness of the B/W kinescope recording, or perhaps it's the grayness of the culture. Pathetic sets and graphics. Animal exploitation (monkeys) for laughs. No wonder alcoholism was so pervasive then. Really makes me appreciate 2016.

I was a kid when this show was made, but seeing the cast of the then Today Show brings back a lot of memories: I used to watch it every morning. This cast is rather historic; the news includes the general public's initial introduction to computers and transistors. Contrary to the previous reviewer, there is no more news of wars on this show than there is currently. People look "50+ years old because most of them were, and fashions were different then. Younger people worked. This news is much more informative: you have real stories from Europe and Africa that would not appear on dumbed-down…

0103_Pork_People_Like_15_44_05_00: Illustrates the different qualities of pork and shows how to acquire the best in meat purchases. Explains the importance of a "meat" type hog, with the necessary steps to raise it, and distinguishes it from the "fat" type. Instructs the housewife in the selection of good meat for her table.

rv: With A title like THAT, how can you NOT like this? Actually, this is a pretty good exploration of what the buyer looks for when buying hogs. Made (I guess) for hog producers the film starts off bubbly with chipper music playing off. I almost thought this was going to be for kids! lol. Luckily we're spared grisly slaughter details but we do get a nice examination of a crosssliced pig, tail still attached! We find out the differences between fat and nonfat pigs. Pretty wild.

The Prelinger Archive has long been known for bringing ephermerial films to the masses. But this piece is just a quirkly little jem. This film, shot between Santa Cruz and San Jose, California some time in the mid-1980s (circa 1986 going by some of the car models and designs), is the film for a driving simulator. The best part is how the film is shot; rather than smooth motion, it is done with a rapid stop-motion, giving the drive along state routes 9 and 135 a surreal feeling. Add the time code at the bottom (for the computer to choose the best scanerio), and you have great bit of source…

This would definitely qualify as an orphan film, and I would be delighted to see more films like these here. Basically, films that aren't produced for audience viewing, unlike the majority of films on this site, but super-specialized ones like this. Films that are along the lines of scientific/industrial/medical/technological, (i.e., industrial x-ray cineflouroscope films of metal fatigue tests, ultra-slow motion test films, thermographic FLIR films, even flight simulator films, etc.) Most films like these would probably sound boring to some, but I would love to see these, due to their…
short ride in a fast machine

I hear that CalTrans has gone completly digital--I cannot wait to see what Director Bob Brink can do with this new medium. This work definelty rivals the severely under-appreciated underground films of Tennessee's mountain passes, in circulation for some years now. This approaches perfection in its simplicity.
More Twists and Turns than you can possibly imagine!

While I was awfully critical of this film being included the first time I saw this, like "what is this doing in the archive??" (ooh nasty). After reading the actual description of this, and viewing the film again, I appreciated this film a lot more. It was sort of fun watching them drive crazily all over the place, not really stopping for anything. At the speed they were going, I was waiting for them to careen off a cliff..
That's what I kept looking for. I have to admit I like this film too.

six_murderous_beliefs: A short film from the National Safety Council detailing six commonly held beliefs that can lead to death.

rv: Shockingly hilarious film that tells of warning signs you've probably never heard of, and I am wondering if people heard of them back in the 50's, which I do believe this film is set. All 6 of these have different episodes, and all of them are quite funny, Especially 'The Price Of Progress' and 'The Law Of Averages' where both adults take their agressions out on the young folk. But the killer one is 'When Your Number's Up, it's up', like who actually thinks like that? A MUST SEE on this site!

Unlike most safety films which often tend to highlight the proper safety procedures that are related to a specific activity, Six Murderous Beliefs concerns itself with the faulty rationales that endanger foolhardy individuals. Each "murderous belief" is accompanied by a brief dramatization illustrating the foolish natures of those who eschew caution. One of the more interesting segments, "The Price of Progress," warns people against attempting to justify dangerous and careless actions simply because they may be beneficial to self or others. Several scenes are unintentionally humourous due to…
A film that teaches safety to teenagers. While the dramatization might be somewhat dated, the six points still hold true today.

The scene where the guy is freehanding a crosscut on a table saw is cringe-worthy enough (I'm a woodworker and doing that pretty much guarantees a serious kick back when the blade binds in the cut). The scene where that smug girl gets hit by the car and the narrator chides her for being stupid is great though.

National Safety Council film from 1955 that shows that the way to prevent accidents is to have a bombastic narrator and overdramatic music. Actually, the rather good message, basically that safety is your responsiblity, get illustarted by the six eponymous beliefs, with associated scenes that range from death by automobile to a cramp in a swimming pool. What seems to be more interesting, however, is how poorly this film has aged. While some of the "beliefs" of the title are still around today (Law Of Averages, I'm Lucky, The Other Guy), others seem peculiar to the 1950s (The Price Of…

Pretty good film about the life of the small town doctor. We follow the typical day of the doctor, which includes appointments at his office, house calls and even some time for Home Life. Surprisingly, the film doesn't flinch on the length of very limited social time with his family.

This film opens with firefighting in Japan circa 1930. The footage starts with shots from the annual firefighting festival held in Tokyo, firefighters wearing their traditional Tokugawa era (1600-1868) firefighting uniforms and techniques as well as demonstrating more modern techniques, including motorized fire trucks and asbestos firesuits. There is also a shot of the Matoi, the fire god emblem, being paraded. This section ends with a brief smokey shot of a lumber yard fire in Shinagawa, in the southwest of Tokyo. The final three-quarters of the film is shots of the Paris fire department…

This 30s firefighting film shows us firefighting practices in Japan and Paris. The Japanese footage is most interesting, as it shows us some unusual cultural things, such as the medal-giving ceremony, the decidedly Asian-looking asbestos suits, and effigies of Matoi, the fire god that were believed to protect homes from fire. The Paris footage is pretty standard, featuring demonstrations of various firefighting practices. As with most Stillman films, this has limited entertainment value, but lots of historical interest. Ratings: Camp/Humor Value: **. Weirdness: ***. Historical Interest: ****.…

Not about the singer, and oddly, not about the Adel Hydraulics corperation, the sponsor of this film. This is more about what actually goes on in a hydraulic engine. Now me, not being motor-engine-inclined, couldn't really give two hoots about this, but this is quite brightly animated, so it's got that going for it, and I love the superhero Hydraulic guy here.

But no, kid gets it in the eye, the kid's doctor is outraged, and sees to it to form an eye safety committee, to get everyone aware of potental eye dangers! Keep in mind that I really did think it was more the school's responsibility to keep kids safe, rather then the kid's, but it was a different time.. Anyways, some great "You'll take an eye out!" examples are shown…

rv: Is riding the belt a no-no then?

This film is about do's and don'ts when dealing with conveyor belts (or as the narrator states, belt conveyors) in mines. Who knew? asongformichael: A Song for Michael A story about the intense affection that develops between a little boy who lives in a remote village and a baby elephant which has strayed from its parents, telling how the boy cares for the elephant until it is sold to an animal trader and then makes a long and arduous journey to set the animal free. Setting: the jungle of Cambodia, near the ruins of Angkor-Vat.
thefirsttwentyyearspart2419031904: A selection of films from the Library of Congress "Paper Print" collection restored by Kemp R. Niver. Early dramas produced in Great Britain and distributed in the U.S. by American Mutoscope and Biograph portray the influenced of harsh realism in British films. Includes The Pickpocket, The Child Stealers, Raid on a Coiner's Den, Revenge, A Railway Tragedy, Decoyed, and Rescued by Rover. Musical accompaniment
americanschoolsflunkingthetest: An investigation of the failure of public education in the United States. Points out that research shows that 10 to 20 per cent of students graduating from high school are functionally illiterate. Covers the increasing power of teacher unions and the lack of effective evaluation and in-service training for teachers
moralitytheprocessofmoraldevelopment: Dr. Susan De Merrsemen-Warren and Dr. Elliot Turiel interview and test children from the age of four until early adulthood in order to examine their concepts of sharing, fairness, justice, and other attitudes linked to the process of moral development
equaljusticeunderlaw1807unitedstatesvaar: A dramatizion of a landmark case heard by the Supreme Court of Chief Justice John Marshall: Should the president have to appear in court when a judge requires him to be a witness? Is an accused traitor entitled to all constitutionally guaranteed fair trial rights? Marshall stepped between Burr and death, closing the doors against government abuse of the treason charge and limiting executive privilege
